title: A monthly water-balance model removed 20-45% of the post-1997 runoff deficits in south-east Australia and the eastern US; the Australian deficit grew gradually from before 1981 without a 1997 step
abstract:
Question: earlier SCI work found that runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU) and the eastern US (East-US) fell 40-50 mm/yr below each catchment's 1951-1996 annual rainfall-runoff regression after 1997. Do seasonality, slow storage, snow and warming explain this in a monthly water-balance model? Which one-parameter change predicts post-2009 flow? When did the deficits start?

Approach: abcd monthly model with snow and Hamon PET, calibrated on 1951-1996 for 153 SE-AU, 171 East-US and 224 West-US CAMELS catchments (CAMELS-AUS v2.03 to 2022 with AGCD or SILO rain; USGS flow and nClimGrid to 2025). Seven mechanisms were fitted on 1997-2009 and tested on 2010-end. Post hoc: bias correction, PET and rain-timing decomposition, and a 1952-1980 calibration for timing.

Results: after 2009 the bias-corrected deficits were -31 mm/yr (95% CI -49 to -16) in SE-AU with AGCD and -37 (-50 to -22) in East-US, against -53 and -49 for the annual regression. Thus the model removed 20-45%, mostly through temperature-driven PET. With SILO rain the SE-AU deficit was -8 (-27 to +8). In SE-AU a proportional flow loss (about 31%) predicted best (skill 0.28), but it already had skill 0.18 in a 1989-1996 placebo. No mechanism predicted East-US flow (skill 0.011 or less). With 1952-1980 calibration, the SE-AU deficit grew gradually (-19 mm/yr per decade; 1997 step -7, CI -27 to +6). The East-US deficit started in the 1990s. West-US had no deficit.

Limitations: one model structure and one PET formula; sqrt calibration causes volume bias; decomposition and timing tests are post hoc; no direct vegetation, dam or groundwater data.
